trend_source: A US creator's clip on investing in yourself (education, health, skills, earning potential) pulled 888.4k views and 210.8k likes, proving the 'you are your greatest asset' message resonates hard.
title: Your biggest asset isn't your HDB or your portfolio. It's you.
hooks: Before I bought a single dollar of any investment, I invested in the one asset I can never sell: me.
Everyone asks me what to invest in first. My honest answer surprises them.
The highest return I ever got wasn't from a fund. It was a course that raised my income.
talking_points: Your earning power is the engine behind every financial goal, so skills and health come before any product.
Protecting that engine matters too: income protection and health coverage exist because your ability to earn is your real asset.
Small reinvestments in yourself compound like money does, and a higher income makes CPF, SRS and saving far easier.
Balance is key: invest in yourself and put a system around the income you create so one setback doesn't undo it.
cta: Comment GROW and I'll share a simple worksheet to protect and grow your biggest asset.
why_it_works: The original went viral on a message advisors genuinely believe, and it lets us bridge honestly from self-worth to income protection without hype.
how_to_film: Talk straight to camera, medium close-up. Open with the hook flat and confident, then count off 'your skills, your health, your income' on your fingers. Keep it under 30 seconds, warm tone.

hooks: There's a viral formula that says your car should cost 5x your salary. In Singapore, COE laughs at that.
I tried these money multiplier rules with SGD prices and one of them completely breaks here.
Multiply your salary by 300 and you get the number that means you never have to work again.
talking_points: Rules of thumb are starting points, not gospel, and Singapore's property and COE prices bend some of them.
The 'freedom number' idea (roughly annual spending times 25) is a useful goal to reverse-engineer your CPF, SRS and investing plan.
A guilt-free spending slice keeps a budget sustainable, so build it in instead of feeling bad about every dollar.
Treat the outputs as targets to close the gap on, then check real numbers against your own income and goals.
cta: Save this and DM me RULES if you want to pressure-test these against your own numbers.
why_it_works: The format is already proven and shareable, and localising the multipliers to SGD gives honest value instead of copying foreign figures.
how_to_film: Fast cuts, one rule per line with the number on screen. Lead with the car-COE hook for a local laugh, keep energy high and pacing snappy.
author: @justtonch

Someone asked me for the Singapore version of the 'financial literacy 101' list. Let's fix it.

Beginner investing here often starts with broad, low-cost diversified funds rather than picking single stocks.
Frame the goal, not the product: emergency cash, protection, then long-term investing in that order.

trend_source: A storytelling clip on why 95% of rich families lose wealth by the third generation earned 68k views and 676 shares on a strong story about passing down systems, not money.
title: Grandfather builds, son spends, grandson begs. How to break the cycle here.
hooks: There's a saying: the grandfather builds, the son spends, the grandson begs. It's scarier than it sounds.
Most family wealth disappears in three generations, and it's rarely the market's fault.
Rich families that last for centuries never pass down money. They pass down something else.
talking_points: Wealth vanishes when heirs inherit assets but never inherit money skills, so teach management before transferring anything.
In Singapore this means talking openly about CPF, property, investments and insurance as a family, not keeping it secret.
Structure matters: a will, clear beneficiary nominations and a plan beat a lump sum handed over blind.
Legacy and estate planning turns 'money' into a 'system' that survives you, so start the conversation early.
cta: DM me LEGACY if you want a simple family money conversation starter.
why_it_works: The proverb and story are gripping and universally true, giving an honest bridge to estate and legacy planning without fear-mongering.
how_to_film: Tell it as a story to camera, slower and deliberate. Open with the 'grandfather builds' line, pause on it, then land the 'systems not money' twist.
author: @wealth_xplained

trend_source: A US skit on hidden dealership 'that's why' fees, ending with a $25k loan at 7.2% ballooning the total cost, hit 57.1k views and 3.9k likes by exposing how loan interest inflates a car's real price.
title: The sticker price is never the real price of your car
hooks: You see 30k on the windscreen. By the time you're done paying, it's a very different number.
The car's price tag is the smallest number in the whole deal. Here's what actually adds up.
Loan interest is the fee nobody puts on the sticker, and in Singapore it quietly adds thousands.
talking_points: The advertised price ignores financing, so a loan's interest rate and tenure change what you truly pay.
In Singapore, factor in COE, road tax, insurance, parking and petrol, not just the monthly instalment.
A longer loan means lower monthly pain but a bigger total, so run the full number before you sign.
Ask yourself what that extra interest could have done if invested or kept in your safety net instead.
cta: Save this before you visit a showroom, and DM me CAR to run your true cost.
why_it_works: The comedic 'that's why' fees hook is memorable and the maths is real, letting us teach total cost of ownership honestly for a local car market.
how_to_film: Keep the escalating-number energy of the original: start at the sticker price, then stack each hidden cost with an on-screen running total. Light, slightly exasperated tone.
author: @itsbobbyfinn

trend_source: Singapore creator sethisfy's phone-upgrade teaser (Fold7 user waiting for an 'iPhone Duo') exploded to 2.6M views, about 203.5x his usual, showing huge appetite for new-phone hype.
title: The real cost of upgrading your phone every year
hooks: I love a new phone as much as anyone, but I did the maths on upgrading every single year.
A new flagship phone every year is basically a small monthly bill you forgot you signed up for.
Before you queue for the newest phone, here's what that habit costs over ten years.
talking_points: New tech is fine if it's budgeted for, so slot it into your guilt-free spending, not your savings.
Yearly upgrades add up: multiply the yearly gap by ten years and picture that same money invested instead.
Financing a phone over 24 months is still a loan, so know the total, not just the monthly.
It's about intention: enjoy the phone on purpose, not on impulse, while your long-term plan keeps running.
cta: Ask yourself in the comments: are you buying the phone, or is FOMO buying it for you?
why_it_works: It rides a massive local phone-hype moment without mocking anyone, turning gadget FOMO into a gentle budgeting lesson.
how_to_film: Hold up your own phone as the prop. Say the hook casually, no judgment, then do quick napkin maths on screen. Keep it playful and self-aware.

Fund the treat from a dedicated bucket, not from your emergency fund or long-term investments.
Time the reward to a milestone you've earned, so it celebrates progress rather than creating debt.
Make sure protection and savings are handled first, then enjoy the reward fully and guilt-free.

Keep investing steadily through rate cycles rather than trying to time the market.
